comments.text: The only factor that everyone leaves out , these earth quakes on the west coast are happening around 37 km below the earth's surface, not on the surface like California!

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: There’s a little more nuance to it. Cascadia isn’t sitting at one fixed depth around 37 km, the plate boundary slopes beneath the continent, and a major rupture can involve a huge area from relatively shallow offshore portions down to much deeper sections. California earthquakes also usually start kilometres underground, even when the fault rupture reaches the surface. The recent quakes I mentioned west of Vancouver Island were actually shallow events within the oceanic plates, not on the Cascadia megathrust.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Exactly, the dead cedar rings were a huge part of dating it. They showed the trees finished growing in 1699 and died before growth began again in 1700. What the rings couldn’t give scientists was the exact day. The January 26, 1700 date came from matching that evidence with written tsunami records from Japan.

comments.text: The big quake in Jan 1700 also match up with a Volcano eruption no one knows about. Glacier Peak.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Interesting connection! Older studies did place some of Glacier Peak’s youngest activity roughly around the 1700s, which puts it near the time of the 1700 Cascadia earthquake. But the dating isn’t precise enough to say they happened together, and current USGS information actually places Glacier Peak’s most recent confirmed eruption much earlier. Still a fascinating rabbit hole to look into.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: This is a fascinating suggestion, and I’m definitely writing it down. I looked into Mica Dam and The Wave, and there’s a real story here, Mica is a massive earthfill dam holding back one of B.C.’s largest reservoirs, and the novel really did imagine a chain of dam failures down the Columbia. I’d want to separate the fictional scenario from the actual engineering and seismic evidence, though, because I haven’t found evidence that a Cascadia quake is expected to collapse Mica. A deep dive into what would actually happen if Mica failed could make a great Hidden Canada video. Thanks for the idea!

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: You’re right that Nanaimo has extensive abandoned coal workings beneath parts of the city, and subsidence is a real hazard the city monitors. But I haven’t found evidence supporting the idea that most of the city would collapse into the mines during a Cascadia earthquake. The 3,400-death figure in the video comes from B.C.’s official 2025 magnitude-nine scenario assessment, so I used their model rather than trying to estimate casualties myself. If you’ve seen a study specifically modelling the old mines during a Cascadia event, I’d genuinely like to read it.
